a phase 2a, double-blind, placebo-controlled, randomised,
adaptive Bayesian trial
Tom P Freeman, Chandni Hindocha, Gianluca Baio, Natacha D C Shaban, Emily M Thomas, Danica Astbury, Abigail M Freeman, Rachel Lees,

Summary
Background A substantial and unmet clinical need exists for pharmacological treatment of cannabis use disorders.
Cannabidiol could offer a novel treatment, but it is unclear which doses might be efficacious or safe. Therefore, we
aimed to identify efficacious doses and eliminate inefficacious doses in a phase 2a trial using an adaptive Bayesian design.
Methods We did a phase 2a, double-blind, placebo-controlled, randomised, adaptive Bayesian trial at the Clinical
Psychopharmacology Unit (University College London, London, UK). We used an adaptive Bayesian dose-finding
design to identify efficacious or inefficacious doses at a-priori interim and final analysis stages. Participants meeting
cannabis use disorder criteria from DSM-5 were randomly assigned (1:1:1:1) in the first stage of the trial to
4-week treatment with three different doses of oral cannabidiol (200 mg, 400 mg, or 800 mg) or with matched placebo
during a cessation attempt by use of a double-blinded block randomisation sequence. All participants received a brief
psychological intervention of motivational interviewing. For the second stage of the trial, new participants were
randomly assigned to placebo or doses deemed efficacious in the interim analysis. The primary objective was
to identify the most efficacious dose of cannabidiol for reducing cannabis use. The primary endpoints were lower
urinary 11-nor-9-carboxy-δ-9-tetrahydrocannabinol (THC-COOH):creatinine ratio, increased days per week with
abstinence from cannabis during treatment, or both, evidenced by posterior probabilities that cannabidiol is better
than placebo exceeding 0·9. All analyses were done on an intention-to-treat basis. This trial is registered with
ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT02044809) and the EU Clinical Trials Register (2013-000361-36).
Findings Between May 28, 2014, and Aug 12, 2015 (first stage), 48 participants were randomly assigned to
placebo (n=12) and to cannabidiol 200 mg (n=12), 400 mg (n=12), and 800 mg (n=12). At interim analysis, cannabidiol
200 mg was eliminated from the trial as an inefficacious dose. Between May 24, 2016, and Jan 12, 2017 (second stage),
randomisation continued and an additional 34 participants were allocated (1:1:1) to cannabidiol 400 mg (n=12),
cannabidiol 800 mg (n=11), and placebo (n=11). At final analysis, cannabidiol 400 mg and 800 mg exceeded primary
endpoint criteria (0·9) for both primary outcomes. For urinary THC-COOH:creatinine ratio, the probability of being the
most efficacious dose compared with placebo given the observed data was 0·9995 for cannabidiol 400 mg and 0·9965
for cannabidiol 800 mg. For days with abstinence from cannabis, the probability of being the most efficacious dose
compared with placebo given the observed data was 0·9966 for cannabidiol 400 mg and 0·9247 for cannabidiol 800 mg.
Compared with placebo, cannabidiol 400 mg decreased THC-COOH:creatinine ratio by -94·21 ng/mL (95% interval
estimate -161·83 to -35·56) and increased abstinence from cannabis by 0·48 days per week (0·15 to 0·82). Compared
with placebo, cannabidiol 800 mg decreased THC-COOH:creatinine ratio by -72·02 ng/mL (-135·47 to -19·52) and
increased abstinence from cannabis by 0·27 days per week (-0·09 to 0·64). Cannabidiol was well tolerated, with no
severe adverse events recorded, and 77 (94%) of 82 participants completed treatment.
Interpretation In the first randomised clinical trial of cannabidiol for cannabis use disorder, cannabidiol 400 mg and
800 mg were safe and more efficacious than placebo at reducing cannabis use.

sections.excerpt: 1.1 Signalling questions Inclusion of signalling questions within each domain of bias is a key feature of RoB 2. Signalling questions aim to elicit information relevant to an assessment of risk of bias. They seek to be reasonably factual in nature. Responses to these questions feed into algorithms we have developed to guide users of the tool to judgements about the risk of bias. The response options for the signalling questions are: (1) Yes; (2) Probably yes; (3) Probably no; (4) No; (5) No information; To maximize the signalling questions’ simplicity and clarity, they are phrased such that a response of ‘Yes’ may be indicative of either a low or high risk of bias, depending on the most natural way to ask the question. Responses of ‘Yes’ and ‘Probably yes’ have the same implications for risk of bias, as do responses of ‘No’ and ‘Probably no’. The definitive versions (‘Yes’ and ‘No’) would typically imply that firm evidence is available in relation to the signalling question; the ‘Probably’ versions would typically imply that a judgement has been made. If review authors calculate measures of agreement (e.g. kappa statistics) for the answers to the signalling questions, we recommend treating ‘Yes’ and ‘Probably yes’ as the same response and ‘No’ and ‘Probably no’ as the same response. The ‘No information’ response should be used only when both (i) insufficient details are reported to permit a response of ‘Probably yes’ or ‘Probably no’, and (ii) in the absence of these details it would be unreasonable to respond ‘Probably yes’ or ‘Probably no’ in the circumstances of the trial. For example, in the context of a large trial run by an experienced clinical trials unit, absence of specific information about generation of the randomization sequence, in a paper published in a journal with rigorously enforced word count limits, is likely to result in a response of ‘Probably yes’ rather than ‘No information’ to the signalling question about sequence generation. The implications for risk of bias judgements of a ‘No information’ response to a signalling question differ according to the purpose of the question. If the question seeks to identify evidence of a problem, then ‘No information’ corresponds to no evidence of that problem. If the question relates to an item that is expected to be reported (such as whether any participants were lost to follow up), then the absence of information leads to concerns about there being a problem. For signalling questions that are answered only if the response to a previous question implies that they are required, a response option ‘Not applicable’ is available. Signalling questions should be answered independently: the answer to one question should not affect answers to other questions in the same or other domains other than through determining which subsequent questions are answered. 1.1.1 Free-text boxes alongside signalling questions The tool provides space for free text alongside the signalling question. In some instances, when the same information is likely to be used to answer more than one question, one text box covers more than one question. These boxes should be used to provide support for the answer to each signalling question. Brief direct quotations from the text of the study report should be used whenever possible.

Randomization provides a fair comparison between two or more intervention groups by balancing, on average, the distribution of known and unknown prognostic factors at baseline between the intervention groups. Missing measurements of the outcome, for example due to dropout during the study, may lead to bias in the intervention effect estimate. Possible reasons for missing outcome data include (83): • participants withdraw from the study or cannot be located (‘loss to follow-up’ or ‘dropout’); • participants do not attend a study visit at which outcomes should have been measured; • participants attend a study visit but do not provide relevant data; • data or records are lost or are unavailable for other reasons; and • participants can no longer experience the outcome, for example because they have died. This domain addresses risk of bias due to missing outcome data, including biases introduced by procedures used to impute, or otherwise account for, the missing outcome data. Some participants may be excluded from an analysis for reasons other than missing outcome data. In particular, a naïve ‘per protocol’ analysis is restricted to participants who received the intended intervention (see section 1.3.1). Potential bias introduced by such analyses, or by other exclusions of eligible participants for whom outcome data are available, is addressed in the domain ‘Bias due to deviations from intended interventions’ (see section 5), in which the final signalling questions examine whether the analysis approach was appropriate. This is a notable change from the previous Cochrane RoB tool for randomized trials, in which the domain addressing bias due to incomplete outcome data addressed both genuinely missing data and data deliberately excluded by the trial investigators.

6.3 Using this domain of the tool (1) Risk of bias will be low if outcome data are available for all, or nearly all, randomized participants. The meaning of ‘nearly all’ in this context is that the number of participants with missing outcome data is so small that their outcomes, whatever they were, could have made no important difference to the estimated effect of intervention. If this is the case then no further signalling questions need be answered. Absence of information about the extent of missing outcome data (for example, when no CONSORT flow diagram was provided in the trial report) will usually lead to a judgement of high risk of bias for this domain. (2) Risk of bias will be low if sensitivity analyses, conducted by either the trial investigators or the review authors (see section 6.1.7), confirm that the finding is robust to plausible values of the missing outcome data. Such analyses are likely to be particularly useful when the amount of missing data is sufficiently large for the potential impact on the estimated effect of intervention to be substantial. If sensitivity analyses confirm that the result is robust, then the result may be regarded as at low risk of bias and no further signalling questions need be answered. (3) As explained in section 6.1.3, missing outcome data can only lead to bias if the chance that the outcome is missing depends on its true value. It may be possible to exclude this based on reported reasons for missing outcome data (for example, if outcome data are only missing because of failure of a measuring instrument or closure of a centre in a multicentre trial). However, if it is possible that missingness in the outcome could depend on its true value then review investigators will need to consider the proportions of and reasons for missing outcome data. (4) A difference between the experimental and comparator intervention groups in the proportions of missing outcome data may indicate a risk of bias (see section 6.1.4). For time-to-event-data, review authors should consider whether rates of censoring (loss to follow-up) differ between the intervention groups. (5) Either reasons for missing outcome data reported by trial investigators, or the circumstances of the trial, may lead review authors to conclude that it is likely that missingness in the outcome depended on its true value. (6) Differing reasons for missing outcome data in the experimental and comparator intervention groups may lead to substantial bias. For example, in a trial of an experimental intervention aimed at smoking cessation there would be serious bias if some comparator intervention participants left the study due to a lack of enthusiasm at receiving nothing novel (and continued to smoke) while some experimental intervention participants left the study due to successful cessation of smoking.

sections.excerpt: The appropriate study population for an analysis of the intention to treat effect is all randomized participants. “Nearly all” should be interpreted as that the number of participants with missing outcome data is sufficiently small that their outcomes, whatever they were, could have made no important difference to the estimated effect of intervention. For continuous outcomes, availability of data from 95% of the participants will often be sufficient. For dichotomous outcomes, the proportion required is directly linked to the risk of the event. If the observed number of events is much greater than the number of participants with missing outcome data, the bias would necessarily be small. Only answer ‘No information’ if the trial report provides no information about the extent of missing outcome data. This situation will usually lead to a judgement that there is a high risk of bias due to missing outcome data. Note that imputed data should be regarded as missing data, and not considered as ‘outcome data’ in the context of this question.

sections.source_locator: Full guidance p. 45, Box 8, signalling question 3.2
sections.excerpt: Evidence that the result was not biased by missing outcome data may come from: (1) analysis methods that correct for bias; or (2) sensitivity analyses showing that results are little changed under a range of plausible assumptions about the relationship between missingness in the outcome and its true value. However, imputing the outcome variable, either through methods such as ‘last-observation-carried-forward’ or via multiple imputation based only on intervention group, should not be assumed to correct for bias due to missing outcome data.

sections.source_locator: Full guidance p. 45, Box 8, signalling question 3.3
sections.excerpt: If loss to follow up, or withdrawal from the study, could be related to participants’ health status, then it is possible that missingness in the outcome was influenced by its true value. However, if all missing outcome data occurred for documented reasons that are unrelated to the outcome then the risk of bias due to missing outcome data will be low (for example, failure of a measuring device or interruptions to routine data collection). In time-to-event analyses, participants censored during trial follow-up, for example because they withdrew from the study, should be regarded as having missing outcome data, even though some of their follow up is included in the analysis. Note that such participants may be shown as included in analyses in CONSORT flow diagrams.

sections.excerpt: This question distinguishes between situations in which (i) missingness in the outcome could depend on its true value (assessed as ‘Some concerns’) from those in which (ii) it is likely that missingness in the outcome depended on its true value (assessed as ‘High risk of bias’). Five reasons for answering ‘Yes’ are: 1. Differences between intervention groups in the proportions of missing outcome data. If there is a difference between the effects of the experimental and comparator interventions on the outcome, and the missingness in the outcome is influenced by its true value, then the proportions of missing outcome data are likely to differ between intervention groups. Such a difference suggests a risk of bias due to missing outcome data, because the trial result will be sensitive to missingness in the outcome being related to its true value. For time-to-event-data, the analogue is that rates of censoring (loss to follow-up) differ between the intervention groups. 2. Reported reasons for missing outcome data provide evidence that missingness in the outcome depends on its true value; 3. Reported reasons for missing outcome data differ between the intervention groups; 4. The circumstances of the trial make it likely that missingness in the outcome depends on its true value. For example, in trials of interventions to treat schizophrenia it is widely understood that continuing symptoms make drop out more likely. 5. In time-to-event analyses, participants’ follow up is censored when they stop or change their assigned intervention, for example because of drug toxicity or, in cancer trials, when participants switch to second-line chemotherapy. Answer ‘No’ if the analysis accounted for participant characteristics that are likely to explain the relationship between missingness in the outcome and its true value.

67|Summary
68|Background A substantial and unmet clinical need exists for pharmacological treatment of cannabis use disorders.
69|Cannabidiol could offer a novel treatment, but it is unclear which doses might be efficacious or safe. Therefore, we
70|aimed to identify efficacious doses and eliminate inefficacious doses in a phase 2a trial using an adaptive Bayesian design.
71|Methods We did a phase 2a, double-blind, placebo-controlled, randomised, adaptive Bayesian trial at the Clinical
72|Psychopharmacology Unit (University College London, London, UK). We used an adaptive Bayesian dose-finding
73|design to identify efficacious or inefficacious doses at a-priori interim and final analysis stages. Participants meeting
74|cannabis use disorder criteria from DSM-5 were randomly assigned (1:1:1:1) in the first stage of the trial to
75|4-week treatment with three different doses of oral cannabidiol (200 mg, 400 mg, or 800 mg) or with matched placebo
76|during a cessation attempt by use of a double-blinded block randomisation sequence. All participants received a brief
77|psychological intervention of motivational interviewing. For the second stage of the trial, new participants were
78|randomly assigned to placebo or doses deemed efficacious in the interim analysis. The primary objective was
79|to identify the most efficacious dose of cannabidiol for reducing cannabis use. The primary endpoints were lower
80|urinary 11-nor-9-carboxy-δ-9-tetrahydrocannabinol (THC-COOH):creatinine ratio, increased days per week with
81|abstinence from cannabis during treatment, or both, evidenced by posterior probabilities that cannabidiol is better
82|than placebo exceeding 0·9. All analyses were done on an intention-to-treat basis. This trial is registered with
83|ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT02044809) and the EU Clinical Trials Register (2013-000361-36).
84|Findings Between May 28, 2014, and Aug 12, 2015 (first stage), 48 participants were randomly assigned to
85|placebo (n=12) and to cannabidiol 200 mg (n=12), 400 mg (n=12), and 800 mg (n=12). At interim analysis, cannabidiol
86|200 mg was eliminated from the trial as an inefficacious dose. Between May 24, 2016, and Jan 12, 2017 (second stage),
87|randomisation continued and an additional 34 participants were allocated (1:1:1) to cannabidiol 400 mg (n=12),
88|cannabidiol 800 mg (n=11), and placebo (n=11). At final analysis, cannabidiol 400 mg and 800 mg exceeded primary
89|endpoint criteria (0·9) for both primary outcomes. For urinary THC-COOH:creatinine ratio, the probability of being the
90|most efficacious dose compared with placebo given the observed data was 0·9995 for cannabidiol 400 mg and 0·9965
91|for cannabidiol 800 mg. For days with abstinence from cannabis, the probability of being the most efficacious dose
92|compared with placebo given the observed data was 0·9966 for cannabidiol 400 mg and 0·9247 for cannabidiol 800 mg.
93|Compared with placebo, cannabidiol 400 mg decreased THC-COOH:creatinine ratio by -94·21 ng/mL (95% interval
94|estimate -161·83 to -35·56) and increased abstinence from cannabis by 0·48 days per week (0·15 to 0·82). Compared
95|with placebo, cannabidiol 800 mg decreased THC-COOH:creatinine ratio by -72·02 ng/mL (-135·47 to -19·52) and
96|increased abstinence from cannabis by 0·27 days per week (-0·09 to 0·64). Cannabidiol was well tolerated, with no
97|severe adverse events recorded, and 77 (94%) of 82 participants completed treatment.
98|Interpretation In the first randomised clinical trial of cannabidiol for cannabis use disorder, cannabidiol 400 mg and
99|800 mg were safe and more efficacious than placebo at reducing cannabis use.

102|Introduction
103|Cannabis is increasingly being legalised for medicinal
104|and recreational use. The long-term effects of these
105|policy reforms are unclear, but might include substantial
106|changes to the types of cannabis products sold and their
107|availability to millions of people worldwide.1 When
108|considering the potential health effects of cannabis use,
109|its largest contribution to the global burden of disease is
110|the impact of cannabis use disorders, which affect an
111|estimated 22 million people worldwide-similar to the
112|prevalence of opioid use disorders.2
113|Δ-9-tetrahydrocannabinol (THC), a partial cannabinoid
114|receptor agonist, is the primary cannabinoid in cannabis
115|products and causes dose-dependent intoxicating and

16|reinforcing effects.1 Studies in Europe3 and the USA4
17|reported a doubling in THC concentrations in cannabis
18|during the past decade. Use of products with higher THC
19|concentrations has been associated with a greater severity
20|of cannabis use disorder5,6 and increases in the incidence
21|of treated cannabis use disorders.7 In the past two decades,
22|the proportion of people seeking treatment for cannabis
23|use disorders has risen in all world regions apart from
24|Africa.8 Cannabis is now the primary drug cited by first-
25|time clients presenting at addiction services across
26|Europe, having increased by 76% in the past decade.9
27|Daily use of cannabis with high THC concentrations is
28|associated with a five-times increased risk of psychosis.10
29|Despite the substantial and increasing demand for
30|treatment, no pharmacotherapies are recommended for
31|the treatment of cannabis use disorders.11
32|Cannabidiol is another cannabinoid found in many
33|cannabis products.4 Cannabidiol has minimal direct
34|action at cannabinoid receptors but it has broad pharma
35|cological actions, including inhibiting the hydrolysis and
36|reuptake of endocannabinoids12 and negative allosteric
37|modulation of cannabinoid receptors.13 Cannabidiol has
38|generated substantial interest because of its potential
39|medicinal uses14 and ability to interact with the effects of
40|THC.15 Cannabidiol has shown therapeutic effects in
41|humans and preclinical models of addiction by reducing
42|the effect of drug-related cues in attentional bias,16,17
43|cue-induced craving,18 and cue-induced reinstatement19
44|paradigms. Collectively, these studies suggest that canna
45|bidiol has potential for treating a range of substance use
46|disorders including cannabis,16 opioids,18,19 and tobacco.17,20
47|A meta-analysis of randomised clinical trials found that
48|cannabidiol was safe and well tolerated with few adverse
49|effects, but interactions with other medications should
50|be monitored carefully because cannabidiol can inhibit
51|cytochrome P450 enzymes.21
52|To our knowledge, no randomised trials have inves
53|tigated cannabidiol as a potential treatment for cannabis
54|use disorder. Open-label case studies have reported that
55|the use of cannabidiol products was associated with
56|reduced cannabis withdrawal symptoms during cannabis
57|abstinence.22,23 A 10-week open-label trial found that
58|cannabidiol administration was associated with improve
59|ments in psychological wellbeing and cognition in
60|regular users of cannabis who were not engaged in a
61|cessation attempt.24 A combination of THC and canna
62|bidiol at 1:1 ratio (nabiximols) has been found to reduce
63|cannabis withdrawal symptoms, cannabis use, or both in
64|some randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled
65|trials.25-27 However, the causal role of cannabidiol in these
66|studies is unclear because they either used an open-label
67|design22-24 or co-administered THC with cannabidiol.25-27
68|Studies in humans28 and in rat29 models of anxiety
69|have reported inverted-U shaped dose-response effects
70|of cannabidiol. These findings highlight the importance
71|of doing an initial dose-finding trial when investigating
72|a novel indication for cannabidiol. Trials testing a single
73|dose against placebo might not select the most
74|efficacious dose for that indication. Therefore, we did
75|a phase 2a trial to identify potentially efficacious doses
76|and eliminate inefficacious doses using an adaptive
77|Bayesian design. Bayesian methods are advantageous
78|for adaptive clinical trials because of their efficiency,
79|flexibility, and ability to make use of all available
80|evidence in a formal and principled way. As a result,
81|they can reduce the amount of resources and participant
82|burden required when doing clinical trials. Additionally,
83|Bayesian analyses provide direct probabilistic measures
84|of the likelihood of a hypothesis (ie, that a treatment
85|is more efficacious than placebo) given the observed
86|data. As such, they provide results that can be more
87|clinically meaningful than frequentist analyses, which
88|test the likelihood of the observed data given the null
89|hypothesis being true (ie, that a treatment does not
90|differ from placebo). We selected a dose range informed
91|by previous clinical trials of oral cannabidiol30,31
92|of 200 mg, 400 mg, and 800 mg daily for 4 weeks. Our
93|primary objective was to identify which (if any) dose of
94|cannabidiol was most efficacious at reducing cannabis
95|use compared with placebo.
96|Research in context
97|Evidence before the study
98|We searched the Cochrane database and peer-reviewed journal
99|articles in Google Scholar with no language restrictions up to
100|March 12, 2020, using the terms "CBD", "cannabis", and
101|"marijuana". A Cochrane review on pharmacotherapies for
102|cannabis use disorders published in 2019 did not recommend
103|any pharmacotherapies for reducing cannabis use in clinical
104|settings. We found no randomised trials testing cannabidiol
105|as a treatment for cannabis use disorder.
106|Added value of this study
107|To our knowledge, this was the first randomised clinical trial
108|of cannabidiol for the treatment of cannabis use disorder.
109|Using an adaptive Bayesian dose-finding design, we showed
110|that at daily oral doses of 400 mg and 800 mg, cannabidiol
111|was a safe and efficacious treatment for reducing cannabis
112|use in people with a cannabis use disorder, assessed by both
113|biological and self-reported measures.
114|Implications of all the available evidence
115|Cannabidiol at daily oral doses of 400 mg and 800 mg has
116|potential to address the substantial and currently unmet clinical
117|need for a pharmacological treatment of cannabis use disorders.

4|Methods
5|Study design and participants
6|We did a phase 2a, randomised, double-blind, placebo-
7|controlled, parallel group clinical trial to investigate
8|cannabidiol as a pharmacological treatment for cannabis
9|use disorder. The trial was done at the Clinical Psycho
10|pharmacology Unit (University College London, London,
11|UK) and was approved by the UK Health Research
12|Authority (13/EE/0303) and the UK Medicines and
13|Healthcare Regulatory Agency (20363/0325/001-0001).
14|We did the trial according to Good Clinical Practice and
15|reported

19|CONSORT
20|checklist
21|(appendix pp 1-3; the protocol is available online).
22|Participants were recruited through advertisements on
23|websites, forums, and flyers in the local community. We
24|initially intended to restrict eligibility to individuals aged
25|16-26 years with vital signs in normal limits, but we
26|removed these criteria early in the first stage of the trial to
27|increase the generalisability of our findings to a wider
28|population who might stand to benefit from this
29|treatment. Participants were included if they were aged
30|16-60 years, met DSM-5 criteria for a cannabis use
31|disorder (of at least moderate severity), and expressed a
32|desire to stop using cannabis and intended to do so in the
33|next month, based on an adapted Motivation To Stop
34|Scale.32 Participants were additionally required to report
35|one or more unsuccessful quit attempts for their cannabis
36|use; report co-administering their cannabis together with
37|tobacco, which is the most common method of using
38|cannabis in Europe,33 provide a urine sample positive for
39|11-nor-9-carboxy-THC (THC-COOH; urine cup 10A,
40|assessing methamphetamine, cocaine, THC, benzodiaze
41|pines, tricyclic antidepressants, barbiturates, phen
42|cyclidine, amphetamines, morphine, and methadone;
43|Alere Toxicology, Abingdon, UK); and have capacity to give
44|written informed consent as defined by Good Clinical
45|Practice guidelines.
46|Women of childbearing potential were required to
47|have a negative pregnancy test within 7 days of starting
48|treatment. An additional inclusion criterion for women
49|of childbearing potential and all men was to use an
50|effective method of contraception including oral,
51|injected, or implanted hormonal methods of contra
52|ception; placement of an intrauterine system or device;
53|a barrier method of contraception; or true abstinence
54|from the time consent was signed until 6 weeks after
55|treatment discontinuation.
56|Exclusion criteria were current breastfeeding or
57|pregnancy; allergies to cannabidiol, microcrystalline
58|cellulose or gelatine; prescribed psychotropic drug use
59|at screening assessments or during treatment weeks;
60|use of other illicit drugs more than twice per month
61|at screening; evidence of inaccurate self-reported drug
62|use due to a positive urine test for a drug that was not
63|reported during screening assessment; current or pre
64|vious self-reported diagnosis of a psychotic disorder; any
65|physical health problem deemed clinically significant
66|by the investigator team; and not speaking English
67|(because of verbal assessments). All data were collected
68|at the Clinical Psychopharmacology Unit (University
69|College London, London, UK).
70|Randomisation and masking
71|For the first stage of the trial, participants were randomly
72|assigned (1:1:1:1) to parallel treatment groups receiving
73|either cannabidiol in three different daily doses (200 mg,
74|400 mg, or 800 mg) or matched placebo. For the second
75|stage of the trial, new participants were randomly assigned
76|to placebo or doses deemed efficacious in the interim
77|analysis. The randomisation sequence was generated by
78|the trial statistician (GB) by use of block randomisation
79|(R command blockrand) with a block size equivalent to
80|the number of treatment groups in the randomisation
81|code. The randomisation code was held by the emergency
82|unblinding service (Sealed Envelope, London, UK) and
83|the drug manufacturer for labelling before shipping to the
84|trial site. Medication packages were labelled by the
85|manufacturer and sent to the trial site with anonymous
86|participant numbers. All investigators and participants
87|remained masked throughout the duration of the trial.
88|Only masked investigators enrolled participants, assigned
89|participants to interventions, did assessments, and
90|entered data. Unmasking did not occur until after the
91|database had been locked by the trial statistician.
92|Procedures
93|Synthetic cannabidiol (99·9% purity) was obtained from
94|STI Pharmaceuticals (Brentwood, UK) and manufactured
95|by Nova Laboratories (Leicester, UK). The trial drug was
96|administered in identical size two gelatine capsules
97|containing microcrystalline cellulose filler and canna
98|bidiol (50 mg, 100 mg, or 200 mg) or no cannabidiol
99|(placebo). After a telephone screening and a screening
100|visit to determine eligibility, participants engaged in a
101|cannabis cessation attempt scheduled to begin at their
102|baseline visit (week 0). At the end of their baseline visit,
103|participants were randomly assigned to treatment groups
104|and instructed to take two capsules twice daily to achieve
105|the daily doses of placebo (capsules with no cannabidiol)
106|and of cannabidiol 200 mg (50 mg capsules), 400 mg
107|(100 mg capsules), and 800 mg (200 mg capsules)
108|for 4 weeks. The bioavailability of oral cannabidiol is
109|increased by food, and twice-daily administration is
110|recommended on the basis of pharmacokinetic and
111|safety data.34 Participants attended site visits weekly
112|during treatment (weeks 1-4), arranged at a time that was
113|most convenient for each participant. Follow-up occurred
114|at weeks 6 (site visit), 8 (telephone), 12 (site visit), 16 (site
115|visit), 20 (telephone), and 24 (telephone).
116|Participants received scheduled text messages twice
117|daily reminding them to take their medication, spaced
118|12 h apart. Dosette boxes were provided for each week
119|of treatment to aid adherence. Adherence was assessed
120|by self-report at weekly assessments as well as by return

41|Outcomes
42|Primary outcomes were cannabis use, as measured in
43|urine (THC-COOH:creatinine ratio) and by self-report
44|(days per week with abstinence from cannabis). These
45|were the two variables that were most strongly associated
46|with cannabis use disorder severity in a study testing
47|15 different biological and self-reported measures of
48|cannabis use.37 Self-reported days with abstinence from
49|cannabis were assessed weekly by use of the timeline
50|follow-back method.38 The primary endpoints were
51|a reduction in urinary THC-COOH:creatinine ratio, an
52|increase in days per week with abstinence from
53|cannabis, or both for cannabidiol versus placebo during
54|treatment, evidenced by posterior probabilities excee
55|ding 0·9. All primary endpoint data were double entered
56|independently by two researchers (TPF and NDCS for
57|the first stage and EMT and DA for the second stage of
58|the trial) and were 100% verified against source data by
59|an independent clinical trial monitor. Reductions
60|in cannabis use up to the final follow-up were analysed
61|as a secondary endpoint.
62|For secondary outcomes, we assessed the total score
63|of the Cannabis Withdrawal Scale39 and tobacco use,
64|assessed in urine (cotinine:creatinine ratio, lower limit of
65|cotinine quantification 1 ng/mL; ABS Laboratories) and
66|by self-report (number of cigarettes smoked using
67|the timeline follow-back method).38 We assessed alcohol
68|consumption using a timeline follow-back38 of each
69|beverage consumed and its alcohol by volume, which
70|was converted to the number of standard UK alcohol
71|units (8 g alcohol). Sleep quality was assessed by use of
72|the total score on the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index.40
73|Depression and anxiety were assessed by use of total
74|scores on the Beck Depression Inventory41 and Beck
75|Anxiety Inventory.42 Secondary endpoints were reduced
76|cannabis withdrawal symptoms, cigarette and alcohol
77|consumption, urinary cotinine:creatinine ratio, depres
78|sion and anxiety symptoms, and improved sleep quality,
79|assessed during the treatment weeks and up to the
80|final follow-up assessment. Additional secondary out
81|comes included cognitive, biological, and physiological
82|measures that will be reported elsewhere.
83|Participants were asked about possible adverse events
84|at each assessment from week 1 to week 16. Adverse
85|events were categorised as mild (does not interfere
86|with the participant's daily routine and does not require
87|intervention; it causes slight discomfort), moderate
88|(interferes with some aspects of daily routine, or requires
89|intervention, but is not damaging to health; it causes
90|moderate discomfort) or severe (results in alteration,
91|discomfort, or disability that is clearly damaging
92|to health). All adverse events were verified with a medical
93|supervisor and an independent trial monitor throughout

45|Discussion
46|To our knowledge, we did the first randomised clinical
47|trial of cannabidiol for the treatment of cannabis use
48|disorder, in which we used an adaptive Bayesian design
49|to establish which (if any) dose of cannabidiol was more
50|efficacious than placebo at reducing cannabis use. We
51|eliminated cannabidiol 200 mg at the first stage and
52|continued randomisation to cannabidiol 400 mg, canna
53|bidiol 800 mg, and placebo treatment groups. At final
54|analysis of the primary endpoints, cannabidiol 400 mg
55|and 800 mg were more efficacious than placebo at
56|reducing cannabis use. These treatment effects were
57|found over and above a brief psychological intervention
58|typically delivered in drug treatment settings.
59|All participants in this trial met a DSM-5 diagnosis of
60|cannabis use disorder. Participants expressed a desire to
61|quit using cannabis in the next month, smoked tobacco
62|with their cannabis, and had not succeeded in quitting
63|cannabis use on at least one previous cessation attempt.
64|This is an important population for whom substantial
65|and rising need for treatment exists8,9 and for whom no
66|pharmacotherapies are recommended at present.11
67|Cannabidiol did not differ from placebo in the number of
68|mild or moderate adverse events at 200 mg, 400 mg,
69|or 800 mg doses. No severe adverse events were recorded,
70|and no participants dropped out because of treatment.
71|The excellent safety and tolerability data and exceptionally
72|high retention rates in our trial suggest that these doses
73|of cannabidiol offer a safe and acceptable treatment for
74|this population.
75|To our knowledge, this is the first adaptive Bayesian
76|dose-finding trial of cannabidiol for a new medical
77|indication. The primary objective of this phase 2a trial
78|was to establish which (if any) dose of cannabidiol was
79|more efficacious than placebo at reducing cannabis use.
80|Cannabidiol 400 mg and 800 mg exceeded the primary
81|endpoint criterion (posterior probability 0·9) for reducing
82|cannabis use during treatment, with converging evidence
83|from biological and self-reported primary outcomes. Our
84|estimates showed that cannabidiol 400 mg and 800 mg
85|both
86|decreased
87|THC-COOH:creatinine
88|ratio
89|and
90|increased abstinence from cannabis.
91|The effects of the cannabidiol doses tested are suggestive
92|of an inverted-U dose-response curve. The 200 mg group
93|was eliminated as an inefficacious dose, and we found
94|some indication that cannabidiol 400 mg was marginally
95|more efficacious than cannabidiol 800 mg. Secondary
96|endpoints showed that the reductions in cannabis use
97|were maintained up to the final follow-up in the canna
98|bidiol 400 mg group but not in the cannabidiol 800 mg
99|group. From a treatment perspective, our findings indicate
100|that cannabidiol doses ranging from 400 mg to 800 mg
101|have the potential to reduce cannabis use in clinical
102|settings, and that additional benefit is unlikely to be gained
103|from doses exceeding 800 mg. It is important to be aware
104|that this dose range (400 mg to 800 mg) is considerably
105|higher than concentrations found in cannabidiol products
106|widely available without a prescription (eg, 25 mg per
107|day).14 These products have inadequate quality assurance
108|and should not be used for medicinal purposes.

4|We observed mixed results for several secondary
5|endpoints, but some findings were consistent across
6|treatment weeks and follow-up. Compared with placebo,
7|cannabidiol 400 mg decreased the number of cigarettes
8|smoked, in line with previous studies of cannabidiol in
9|tobacco smokers.17,20 However, sleep quality was lower in
10|the cannabidiol 400 mg group compared with placebo,
11|which might be interpreted in the context of greater
12|reductions in cannabis use in this group. Compared
13|with placebo, cannabidiol 800 mg reduced cannabis
14|withdrawal symptoms, consistent with previous case
15|reports,22,23 and reduced anxiety symptoms, in line with
16|experimental studies in humans28 and rats.29
17|The key strengths of this study include its novel
18|indication, for which substantial clinical need exists, and
19|its adaptive Bayesian dose-finding design. This design
20|enabled us to test a range of doses in an efficient
21|manner, which would have required considerably greater
22|resources and participant burden when using a typical
23|trial design. In terms of limitations, this phase 2a dose-
24|finding trial was not designed to provide robust esti
25|mates of the magnitude of efficacy. Additional evidence is
26|needed to improve the precision of the estimates obtained
27|in this study. Although we found strong evidence for dose-
28|response effects of cannabidiol on plasma cannabidiol
29|concentrations, factors such as food consumption could
30|have contributed to variation in the bioavailability of
31|cannabidiol. This trial used a 4-week treatment period,
32|consistent with a previous clinical trial for psychosis.30
33|Additional studies are needed to investigate the extent to
34|which these findings translate to different durations
35|of treatment. Additional research is needed to investigate
36|whether cannabidiol reduces cannabis use independently
37|or through mechanisms shared with other mental health
38|symptoms such as anxiety.
39|In conclusion, our trial provides the first causal
40|evidence supporting cannabidiol as a treatment for
41|cannabis use disorders. These findings are important in
42|light of major policy changes surrounding the production
43|and sale of cannabis products, increases in the number
44|of people entering treatment for cannabis use disorders
45|worldwide,8,9 and the absence of recommended pharma

sections.excerpt: 1.1 Signalling questions Inclusion of signalling questions within each domain of bias is a key feature of RoB 2. Signalling questions aim to elicit information relevant to an assessment of risk of bias. They seek to be reasonably factual in nature. Responses to these questions feed into algorithms we have developed to guide users of the tool to judgements about the risk of bias. The response options for the signalling questions are: (1) Yes; (2) Probably yes; (3) Probably no; (4) No; (5) No information; To maximize the signalling questions’ simplicity and clarity, they are phrased such that a response of ‘Yes’ may be indicative of either a low or high risk of bias, depending on the most natural way to ask the question. Responses of ‘Yes’ and ‘Probably yes’ have the same implications for risk of bias, as do responses of ‘No’ and ‘Probably no’. The definitive versions (‘Yes’ and ‘No’) would typically imply that firm evidence is available in relation to the signalling question; the ‘Probably’ versions would typically imply that a judgement has been made. If review authors calculate measures of agreement (e.g. kappa statistics) for the answers to the signalling questions, we recommend treating ‘Yes’ and ‘Probably yes’ as the same response and ‘No’ and ‘Probably no’ as the same response. The ‘No information’ response should be used only when both (i) insufficient details are reported to permit a response of ‘Probably yes’ or ‘Probably no’, and (ii) in the absence of these details it would be unreasonable to respond ‘Probably yes’ or ‘Probably no’ in the circumstances of the trial. For example, in the context of a large trial run by an experienced clinical trials unit, absence of specific information about generation of the randomization sequence, in a paper published in a journal with rigorously enforced word count limits, is likely to result in a response of ‘Probably yes’ rather than ‘No information’ to the signalling question about sequence generation. The implications for risk of bias judgements of a ‘No information’ response to a signalling question differ according to the purpose of the question. If the question seeks to identify evidence of a problem, then ‘No information’ corresponds to no evidence of that problem. If the question relates to an item that is expected to be reported (such as whether any participants were lost to follow up), then the absence of information leads to concerns about there being a problem. For signalling questions that are answered only if the response to a previous question implies that they are required, a response option ‘Not applicable’ is available. Signalling questions should be answered independently: the answer to one question should not affect answers to other questions in the same or other domains other than through determining which subsequent questions are answered. 1.1.1 Free-text boxes alongside signalling questions The tool provides space for free text alongside the signalling question. In some instances, when the same information is likely to be used to answer more than one question, one text box covers more than one question. These boxes should be used to provide support for the answer to each signalling question. Brief direct quotations from the text of the study report should be used whenever possible.

Randomization provides a fair comparison between two or more intervention groups by balancing, on average, the distribution of known and unknown prognostic factors at baseline between the intervention groups. Missing measurements of the outcome, for example due to dropout during the study, may lead to bias in the intervention effect estimate. Possible reasons for missing outcome data include (83): • participants withdraw from the study or cannot be located (‘loss to follow-up’ or ‘dropout’); • participants do not attend a study visit at which outcomes should have been measured; • participants attend a study visit but do not provide relevant data; • data or records are lost or are unavailable for other reasons; and • participants can no longer experience the outcome, for example because they have died. This domain addresses risk of bias due to missing outcome data, including biases introduced by procedures used to impute, or otherwise account for, the missing outcome data. Some participants may be excluded from an analysis for reasons other than missing outcome data. In particular, a naïve ‘per protocol’ analysis is restricted to participants who received the intended intervention (see section 1.3.1). Potential bias introduced by such analyses, or by other exclusions of eligible participants for whom outcome data are available, is addressed in the domain ‘Bias due to deviations from intended interventions’ (see section 5), in which the final signalling questions examine whether the analysis approach was appropriate. This is a notable change from the previous Cochrane RoB tool for randomized trials, in which the domain addressing bias due to incomplete outcome data addressed both genuinely missing data and data deliberately excluded by the trial investigators.

6.3 Using this domain of the tool (1) Risk of bias will be low if outcome data are available for all, or nearly all, randomized participants. The meaning of ‘nearly all’ in this context is that the number of participants with missing outcome data is so small that their outcomes, whatever they were, could have made no important difference to the estimated effect of intervention. If this is the case then no further signalling questions need be answered. Absence of information about the extent of missing outcome data (for example, when no CONSORT flow diagram was provided in the trial report) will usually lead to a judgement of high risk of bias for this domain. (2) Risk of bias will be low if sensitivity analyses, conducted by either the trial investigators or the review authors (see section 6.1.7), confirm that the finding is robust to plausible values of the missing outcome data. Such analyses are likely to be particularly useful when the amount of missing data is sufficiently large for the potential impact on the estimated effect of intervention to be substantial. If sensitivity analyses confirm that the result is robust, then the result may be regarded as at low risk of bias and no further signalling questions need be answered. (3) As explained in section 6.1.3, missing outcome data can only lead to bias if the chance that the outcome is missing depends on its true value. It may be possible to exclude this based on reported reasons for missing outcome data (for example, if outcome data are only missing because of failure of a measuring instrument or closure of a centre in a multicentre trial). However, if it is possible that missingness in the outcome could depend on its true value then review investigators will need to consider the proportions of and reasons for missing outcome data. (4) A difference between the experimental and comparator intervention groups in the proportions of missing outcome data may indicate a risk of bias (see section 6.1.4). For time-to-event-data, review authors should consider whether rates of censoring (loss to follow-up) differ between the intervention groups. (5) Either reasons for missing outcome data reported by trial investigators, or the circumstances of the trial, may lead review authors to conclude that it is likely that missingness in the outcome depended on its true value. (6) Differing reasons for missing outcome data in the experimental and comparator intervention groups may lead to substantial bias. For example, in a trial of an experimental intervention aimed at smoking cessation there would be serious bias if some comparator intervention participants left the study due to a lack of enthusiasm at receiving nothing novel (and continued to smoke) while some experimental intervention participants left the study due to successful cessation of smoking.

sections.excerpt: The appropriate study population for an analysis of the intention to treat effect is all randomized participants. “Nearly all” should be interpreted as that the number of participants with missing outcome data is sufficiently small that their outcomes, whatever they were, could have made no important difference to the estimated effect of intervention. For continuous outcomes, availability of data from 95% of the participants will often be sufficient. For dichotomous outcomes, the proportion required is directly linked to the risk of the event. If the observed number of events is much greater than the number of participants with missing outcome data, the bias would necessarily be small. Only answer ‘No information’ if the trial report provides no information about the extent of missing outcome data. This situation will usually lead to a judgement that there is a high risk of bias due to missing outcome data. Note that imputed data should be regarded as missing data, and not considered as ‘outcome data’ in the context of this question.

sections.excerpt: Evidence that the result was not biased by missing outcome data may come from: (1) analysis methods that correct for bias; or (2) sensitivity analyses showing that results are little changed under a range of plausible assumptions about the relationship between missingness in the outcome and its true value. However, imputing the outcome variable, either through methods such as ‘last-observation-carried-forward’ or via multiple imputation based only on intervention group, should not be assumed to correct for bias due to missing outcome data.

sections.source_locator: Full guidance p. 45, Box 8, signalling question 3.3
sections.excerpt: If loss to follow up, or withdrawal from the study, could be related to participants’ health status, then it is possible that missingness in the outcome was influenced by its true value. However, if all missing outcome data occurred for documented reasons that are unrelated to the outcome then the risk of bias due to missing outcome data will be low (for example, failure of a measuring device or interruptions to routine data collection). In time-to-event analyses, participants censored during trial follow-up, for example because they withdrew from the study, should be regarded as having missing outcome data, even though some of their follow up is included in the analysis. Note that such participants may be shown as included in analyses in CONSORT flow diagrams.

sections.source_locator: Full guidance pp. 45-46, Box 8, signalling question 3.4
sections.excerpt: This question distinguishes between situations in which (i) missingness in the outcome could depend on its true value (assessed as ‘Some concerns’) from those in which (ii) it is likely that missingness in the outcome depended on its true value (assessed as ‘High risk of bias’). Five reasons for answering ‘Yes’ are: 1. Differences between intervention groups in the proportions of missing outcome data. If there is a difference between the effects of the experimental and comparator interventions on the outcome, and the missingness in the outcome is influenced by its true value, then the proportions of missing outcome data are likely to differ between intervention groups. Such a difference suggests a risk of bias due to missing outcome data, because the trial result will be sensitive to missingness in the outcome being related to its true value. For time-to-event-data, the analogue is that rates of censoring (loss to follow-up) differ between the intervention groups. 2. Reported reasons for missing outcome data provide evidence that missingness in the outcome depends on its true value; 3. Reported reasons for missing outcome data differ between the intervention groups; 4. The circumstances of the trial make it likely that missingness in the outcome depends on its true value. For example, in trials of interventions to treat schizophrenia it is widely understood that continuing symptoms make drop out more likely. 5. In time-to-event analyses, participants’ follow up is censored when they stop or change their assigned intervention, for example because of drug toxicity or, in cancer trials, when participants switch to second-line chemotherapy. Answer ‘No’ if the analysis accounted for participant characteristics that are likely to explain the relationship between missingness in the outcome and its true value.

Summary
Background A substantial and unmet clinical need exists for pharmacological treatment of cannabis use disorders.
Cannabidiol could offer a novel treatment, but it is unclear which doses might be efficacious or safe. Therefore, we
aimed to identify efficacious doses and eliminate inefficacious doses in a phase 2a trial using an adaptive Bayesian design.
Methods We did a phase 2a, double-blind, placebo-controlled, randomised, adaptive Bayesian trial at the Clinical
Psychopharmacology Unit (University College London, London, UK). We used an adaptive Bayesian dose-finding
design to identify efficacious or inefficacious doses at a-priori interim and final analysis stages. Participants meeting
cannabis use disorder criteria from DSM-5 were randomly assigned (1:1:1:1) in the first stage of the trial to
4-week treatment with three different doses of oral cannabidiol (200 mg, 400 mg, or 800 mg) or with matched placebo
during a cessation attempt by use of a double-blinded block randomisation sequence. All participants received a brief
psychological intervention of motivational interviewing. For the second stage of the trial, new participants were
randomly assigned to placebo or doses deemed efficacious in the interim analysis. The primary objective was
to identify the most efficacious dose of cannabidiol for reducing cannabis use. The primary endpoints were lower
urinary 11-nor-9-carboxy-δ-9-tetrahydrocannabinol (THC-COOH):creatinine ratio, increased days per week with
abstinence from cannabis during treatment, or both, evidenced by posterior probabilities that cannabidiol is better
than placebo exceeding 0·9. All analyses were done on an intention-to-treat basis. This trial is registered with
ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT02044809) and the EU Clinical Trials Register (2013-000361-36).
Findings Between May 28, 2014, and Aug 12, 2015 (first stage), 48 participants were randomly assigned to
placebo (n=12) and to cannabidiol 200 mg (n=12), 400 mg (n=12), and 800 mg (n=12). At interim analysis, cannabidiol
200 mg was eliminated from the trial as an inefficacious dose. Between May 24, 2016, and Jan 12, 2017 (second stage),
randomisation continued and an additional 34 participants were allocated (1:1:1) to cannabidiol 400 mg (n=12),
cannabidiol 800 mg (n=11), and placebo (n=11). At final analysis, cannabidiol 400 mg and 800 mg exceeded primary
endpoint criteria (0·9) for both primary outcomes. For urinary THC-COOH:creatinine ratio, the probability of being the
most efficacious dose compared with placebo given the observed data was 0·9995 for cannabidiol 400 mg and 0·9965
for cannabidiol 800 mg. For days with abstinence from cannabis, the probability of being the most efficacious dose
compared with placebo given the observed data was 0·9966 for cannabidiol 400 mg and 0·9247 for cannabidiol 800 mg.
Compared with placebo, cannabidiol 400 mg decreased THC-COOH:creatinine ratio by -94·21 ng/mL (95% interval
estimate -161·83 to -35·56) and increased abstinence from cannabis by 0·48 days per week (0·15 to 0·82). Compared
with placebo, cannabidiol 800 mg decreased THC-COOH:creatinine ratio by -72·02 ng/mL (-135·47 to -19·52) and
increased abstinence from cannabis by 0·27 days per week (-0·09 to 0·64). Cannabidiol was well tolerated, with no
severe adverse events recorded, and 77 (94%) of 82 participants completed treatment.
Interpretation In the first randomised clinical trial of cannabidiol for cannabis use disorder, cannabidiol 400 mg and
800 mg were safe and more efficacious than placebo at reducing cannabis use.

automatically simulated from the Bayesian procedure, in accordance with the modelling and
distributional assumptions. In order to test our primary endpoint, THC-COOH/creatinine
concentrations and days per week abstinent from cannabis were analysed during treatment

answers.justification: The report states Bayesian multiple imputation under a missing-at-random assumption and automatic simulation of missing outcomes. This is a model for missing values, not evidence that the result is unbiased under plausible departures from MAR; the described sensitivity analyses add age and sex, not assumptions about missingness. No missingness-specific sensitivity or bias-correction evidence is reported in the inspected passages. Therefore there is probably not evidence that the estimate was protected from missing-data bias.

answers.justification: The outcome measures cannabis use during an active cessation attempt. The flow diagram identifies drop-out, loss to follow-up, missed scheduled visits, and poor adherence as reasons for incomplete treatment. For a behavioral cannabis-use endpoint, disengagement or missed assessment could plausibly be related to continued use or successful cessation, so outcome-dependent missingness cannot reasonably be excluded. The report does not establish that it actually occurred, hence probably yes rather than yes.
